messages.subject: temporally specific predictions across siteCovs in pcountOPEN
parts:
Hi all,
I am currently working on some 15 odd years of nocturnal forest mammal data (from spotlight surveys) using pcountOPEN.  I have 137 sites and 35 primary periods (defined by year/season combinations in which I felt it reasonable to assume closure).  However, I am really interested in differences between two longer time-periods (defined as before and after primary period 20 or so, also coded as "time_step3" in my yearlySiteCovs in my model).  Using the example code from the pcountOPEN documentation I have been able to calculate yearly estimates using ranef() but I would like to do this in a way similar to that acheived using predict(), such that I get predictions across a range of values of MATemp, but averaged over the two groups of primary periods of interest.  Any thoughts on how to do this would be much appreciated.
Cheers
A

(fm37a <- pcountOpen(~MATemp+MATemp2+annual_pptn12, ~time_step3, ~time_step3,
~wet+wind+season+temp_anomaly+moon+decimal_start, spp.umf,
                     K=tk,mixture = "ZIP", dynamics = "constant", se = TRUE))

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: temporally specific predictions across siteCovs in pcountOPEN
parts: This is a tricky task, which is probably why it hasn't been answered.  You'll want to use some code similar to the calculation of N.hat2 in the help file for pcountOpen.  Predict some values for lambda across the MATemp range and then generate N.hat predictions through time using the back-transformed omega and gamma estimates specific to the time periods.  You could then obtain the time period means and plot them across MATemp.  Getting confidence intervals for those means will be more difficult.

messages.author: f0732d7bffc290cf
messages.subject: Re: temporally specific predictions across siteCovs in pcountOPEN
parts:
Hi Dan,
Thanks for your helpful reply.  I have had a go at doing as you suggested, but in the end decided it was simpler to model the time-step effect by splitting my data into the time-steps and stacking site-time_step combinations (as suggested elsewhere by Andy: "...based on stacking data from multiple years on top of each other and basically treating "year x site" as "effective sites").  This has allowed me to produce some plausible models, e.g.:

> (fm36a <- pcountOpen(~MATemp+MATemp2+ time_step3 +MATemp.time_step3 + MATemp2.time_step3,
+                      ~1, ~1, ~wet+wind+season+temp_anomaly+moon+decimal_start, spp.umf,
+                      K=tk,mixture = "ZIP", dynamics = "constant", se = TRUE))

Call:
pcountOpen(lambdaformula = ~MATemp + MATemp2 + time_step3 + MATemp.time_step3 +
    MATemp2.time_step3, gammaformula = ~1, omegaformula = ~1,
    pformula = ~wet + wind + season + temp_anomaly + moon + decimal_start,
    data = spp.umf, mixture = "ZIP", K = tk, dynamics = "constant",
    se = TRUE)

> mod = "fm36a"
> save(fm36a,file = paste(outfolder,spp_folder,mod, sep = ""))

And to generate predictions with confidence intervals for a range of my values of my environmental variable of interest:

> E.psi = predictSE.zip(fm36a, newdata =newData2, se.fit = TRUE, parm.type = "lambda",
+                       type = "lambda", print.matrix = FALSE, c.hat = .25)
>
> E.psi = as.data.frame(E.psi)
> max( E.psi$fit)
[1] 17.78615

But... when I try to use ranef to calculate the site-specific values of lambda,  The maximum values of the most abundant sites are much higher than those for the predictSE.zip estimates:

> load(file = paste(outfolder, spp_folder, "re_36a", sep  =""))
> N.hat0 = bup(re); #head(N.hat0)
> max(N.hat0[,17])
[1] 72.39437

Is this to be expected?  When running ranef() I also get the following error, which I assumed was not important at the time..

> # run ranef and save output
> re <- ranef(fm36a)
Warning message:
In .local(object, ...) :
  Method to compute SE for ZIP model has not been written
and I can then use predictSE.zip from the package AICmodavg to get the some estimation of the error around the estimated lambda values.
 
Any thoughts or suggestions would be much appreciated.
Alex
